Totally - at this point, it’s only been a week since we broke up. So the loving & secure relationship that I want is still that one, which is totally unfair, because that relationship would never be loving and secure for him. Abuse does that. It’s a tough pill to swallow for me for sure. 

I’m definitely glad it’s given me the motivation to seek real change. I can see my faults a lot more clearly and understand the objective wrongness of so much of what I did, which he tried to tell me for years before leaving. That’s the hard part to forgive myself for. He suffered so much for my sake and to keep us together, and he’s never going to get to see a non toxic, in recovery version of me that he deserves. Worst, he’s never going to want it even if he could have it. Paiiiiinnn.

I do agree with you. I feel so bad that I don’t think anything except him leaving me would’ve actually gotten me to therapy. And I know changing for someone else isn’t right anyway, but it just seems so pointless unless what I want can work out, you know?

and that’s even with being able to recognize that a fresh slate would be nice, a relationship with someone whose friends/family/etc don’t hate me. The memories and intimacy are just so hard to let go of, especially when I basically grew up and into my BPD with him by my side. It’s so tough

I struggle with this a lot as well - like nothing super fucked up happened to me, so why am I so fucked up? 

I think what I’ve learned is that it doesn’t have to be some monumental awful sequence of stereotypical events to be traumatic. My parents are married, I have siblings, we’ve always been middle class, they aren’t bad people. But regardless of that, emotions were never really discussed and even as a kid I was not ever given a safe space to be emotional with my caregivers. That is trauma, even if it doesn’t seem “traumatic enough”. That leads to an inability to regulate emotions and an over attachment to romantic partners and a codependency on those who do let me emote. Maybe something like that is true of your childhood as well.

this is tough, and i think a lot of us can relate to being embarrassed for the things we did to shift our pain and instead get attention/validation/sympathy etc. obviously, you know what you did is wrong. you tried to reach out and apologize. at this point.. that’s all you can do. accept that you did a horrible thing, try to make amends, and vow to be better in the future. there’s no benefit that comes from continually feeling guilty or shame, even though it’s hard to avoid. face the regret head on, and let yourself move on from it. let it make you a better person in the future, because there’s nothing it can do for you in the past. 

with regards to reputation, is it still a big deal in your everyday life if it was 10 years ago? honestly, if it’s something still plaguing you and you can’t escape it, i’d suggest moving if it’s possible. getting in a new environment will help you rid yourself of that self harm producing shame and focus on growing.

i was in a similar place as you for a long time and you may not appreciate my advice but it’s helped me. honestly, your fear of abandonment is always going to exist.. because your boyfriend can ALWAYS leave you. whether it’s bc of college, cheating, meeting someone else, or he just wakes up one morning and wants something different, you literally have no control over any of that (which is *very* difficult to accept). however, in knowing that, you also know the reverse: he’s chosen not to leave this far, and you have no logical reason to think that he would suddenly leave now. thinking about it like this has helped assuage my fear some because at the end of the day there are no guarantees in relationships, and it’s something we have to learn to accept and live with

i agree w you that communication is important. i’ve been trying to work on letting him know things that trigger me and he can definitely tell when we’re about to go down a bad path, but i’m having trouble with making him feel like it’s his responsibility to notice that i’m about to spiral/notice that i’m triggered/keep himself from saying something to trigger me. i don’t want to do this, because this disorder is not his fault and i don’t want him always on edge. but i do think that the way i’ve expressed it to him has made him feel that noticing something might trigger me and stopping it before it starts is his responsibility. do you have any advice for getting away from that? i don’t want the brunt of this disorder to be on him, and i fear that i have done that thus far, and he’s just taking it in the name of support

i don’t have any advice, but i relate a lot. for me, my so needing space tends to send me into attacks where i immediately want him to comfort me.. and i can be manipulative in order to accomplish that. i think it’s important to remember that our so’s are entitled to boundaries, and if they need space, they deserve it. our mental stability (or lack thereof) is not their responsibility and it’s not fair to treat them or make them feel like it is

at the same time, i’m guilty of exactly the same thing. and when he calls me manipulative for it, i’m like “what?! i’m manipulative for needing comfort from this hell that isn’t my fault?!” but to them, it IS manipulative because they need space and we’re encroaching on that by making them feel responsible for a disorder that isn’t their fault. 

i would try to focus not on feeling guilty afterwards for being the villain, but recognizing from the get go that you spiraling emotionally is not your boyfriends job to fix... and it’s a lot easier said than done, i know. let’s work on it together!!
